scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance started in the 19th century in Morelos. It was a satirical response to the Spanish hacienda system.
Workers used Carnival to mock their employers. They dressed up and danced to reclaim public spaces once held by the elite.
on_screen: Map: Mexico · North America
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Chinelos is traditionally performed during Carnival.
Now it symbolizes Morelos and appears at Independence Day celebrations, private parties, and religious processions like those for the Niñopa.
It remains a living tradition today.
on_screen: Footage: File:ChinelosExpoIndigenas 11.webm (https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/32/ChinelosExpoIndigenas_11.webm?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=imageinfo&utm_content=original)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance features a repetitive jump called the 'brincon'.
Dancers stand with feet apart and knees slightly bent.
They do two shuffling steps, then a small jump to the right or left, often leading with one shoulder.
Watch for the brincon.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (StD49sFh274)
Captions name each signature move as it appears

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Originally, the dance was accompanied by whistling and improvised percussion.
Today, brass bands provide the music.
Listen for trumpets, trombones, and tubas.
The music is rhythmic and driving, designed to keep the dancers going for long periods.
It is brass-heavy, high-energy, and loud, with repetitive melodies that carry through streets and open spaces.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The costume includes a velvet robe, a mesh mask with an upturned beard, a large plumed hat, and gloves.
These elements mock European colonial fashion and hide the dancer's identity.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Jesús Meza, known as 'Chucho el Muerto', developed early rhythmic sounds for the dance in 1860.
The Banda de Musica Santa Maria de Tlayacapan is the most famous group linked to the tradition.
Tlayacapan is considered the birthplace of the modern form.
The dance blends indigenous and Catholic traditions.
It evolved from mocking 19th-century European salon dancing and the social conditions on sugar cane haciendas.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Chinelos was influenced by the Jota aragonesa.
Hacendados historically performed that dance, which Chinelos began to mock.
